This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place, no matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman. A new court filing details the condition of the Tennessee woman who officials attempted to execute earlier this week. Attorneys for Christa Pike say she was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious as hospital staff worked to save her life and clear the drug the state had administered from her body.
Tony Gonzalez, a member stationed WPLN, has our reports. Christa Pike's legal team wants the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence and is asking a judge for help. They're also citing several months of warnings they had provided about a blood disorder that would make it difficult to insert an IV line.
They were also concerned because prison staff had failed to insert a line during another lethal injection attempt in May. Now they say that the drug pentobarbital could have been sent into Pike's arm instead of her vein. Tennessee has struggled with lethal injections.
Four years ago, officials were found to have ignored protocols and mishandled drugs. The state made changes, but concerns remained and the governor has now ordered another review.
For NPR News, I'm Tony Gonzalez in Nashville.
Democrats are expanding the map of congressional races they say could be winnable next month. As NPR's Tamara Keith reports, the new list now includes 66 districts.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is pushing into traditionally Republican territory, adding districts in Kansas, North Carolina, Texas and Oklahoma, among others, to its districts in playlist.
That is a list of congressional districts where the party committee thinks it can be competitive. It doesn't mean the Democratic candidates in these races have an easy path to victory, but it does mean Democrats are bullish about their chances overall.
Republicans are projecting confidence as well, with Speaker Mike Johnson traveling around the country, saying he thinks his party will expand its House majority.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Both of Brazil's main presidential candidates declined to debate each other on prime-time TV just days before Saturday's general election.
NPR's Kari Khan reports on one of Brazil's tightest contests, with between incumbent Luis Inácio Lula da Silva and facing the son of a former far-right president.
The global TV debate was called up just hours before it was to go live. President Luis Inácio Lula da Silva, the first to bow out, called the debate "pointless" and joined a popular podcast instead.
Conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro decided not to participate after several rulings by Brazil's top electoral court were issued regarding the debate format.
He called it censorship and called Lula a coward.
Justices ruled that Globo could not have an empty podium with Lula's name on stage and that candidates could not ask questions directed to the absent president.
Polls show the race is a statistical dead heat.
If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote, a runoff will be held October 25th.
Kari Khan, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
And this is NPR News.
It was a good day for Wall Street Friday, with stocks rising across the board.
The NASDAQ composite gained 1.2 percent at the close, while the S&P 500 finished up seven-tenths.
That's within one percent of its record high set back in August, and the Dow added a half a percent, or 250 points.
The increases came after the Labor Department announced employers added just 29,000 more jobs in September, down from 133,000 in August.
CBS and the NFL star turned commentator Tony Romo have parted ways.
The move follows Romo's arrest this summer for operating a vehicle while intoxicated, and Piers Becky Sullivan has more.
Back in July, Romo was arrested in Wisconsin after he performed poorly on field sobriety tests, police said.
He had been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017, and that gig, of course, followed his decade-plus-long career as quarterback for the Dallas Cowboys.
After the arrest, Romo apologized and said the multiple back surgeries that ended his career prematurely have left him with "constant debilitating pain,"
which led to a reliance on pain medication and attempts to buck that dependence, he says, led to problems with alcohol.
In a new statement, CBS said the decision to part ways with Romo was mutual.
In Romo's absence this season, the former Houston Texans star J.J. Watt has been filling in.
CBS says Watt will continue in the role.
Becky Sullivan and Piers News.
The owner of the San Francisco 49ers has been suspended for six games and fined $500,000 after being arrested earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio.
The league ruled that Jed York violated the league's personal conduct policy.
York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this year.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
